newsitem.title: USA: Heat briefly slows US Midwest hog movement.
newsitem.headline: Heat briefly slows US Midwest hog movement.

text.p: Hot, muggy weather slowed U.S. hog shipments early Monday in the western Corn Belt and further tightened hog supplies, but conditions were expected to improve as the week progresses, market sources said.
"Today should be the worst day for hogs," said Fred Gesser, chief forecaster for Weather Express Inc in Omaha, Neb.

Temperatures were seen in the upper 80s Fahrenheit in much of Iowa and the low 90s in Illinois, Indiana and western Ohio, Gesser said. But it will feel closer to 105 degrees based on the humidity comfort index, he said.

Interior Iowa and southern Minnesota top prices for hogs delivered to plants near midday Monday were at $59.50 per cwt, up $1.00 from Friday, the U.S. Agriculture Department reported. Estimates for interior hog movement were 90,000 head compared with 91,000 a week ago and 95,000 a year ago, USDA said.

Temperatures were forecast in the upper 70s to low 80s in Iowa and northern Missouri by the end of the week and forecasts for next week called for "fairly warm" temperatures in the mid-80s to low 90s, Gesser said.
"We should get a little bit of a reprieve by the end of this week, but there really is no dome of doom," Gesser said.
"There's a tolerable level of heat. I dont think we're going to have mid-90s or plus. I don't think we're going to have that problem," Gesser said.

Temperatures that range in the upper 90s for several days can have a significant impact on hog weight gains and stress levels, said Glenn Grimes, agricultural economist with the University of Missouri at Columbia.
Although heat and humidity were high during the weekend and on Monday, they were not severe enough to cause concern among hog farmers, Grimes said.
"We haven't had enough days of any material heat across the major hog belt to impact the hogs very much," Grimes said.
When temperatures and humidity do become severe, it can slow hog weight gains and increase stress among hogs being shipped to market, he said.
"Of course most hogs are shipped at night, so that minimizes stress, but you can have greater death loss with the heat and humidity," Grimes said.
"But its really too early yet," Grimes said.
